implementation_notes: The container is the Session Manager: request.getSession(false) validates without creating, HttpSession.getId/getCreationTime/getLastAccessedTime/setMaxInactiveInterval/invalidate cover the life cycle, and the JSESSIONID cookie is the transport. What replaces the classic structure is the container plus its session listener or registry; what remains policy is regeneration on privilege change (request.changeSessionId()), invalidation on logout (invalidate()), timeout configuration and cookie attributes, which the container exposes but does not harden by default.
pitfalls: getSession() without the boolean creates a session on every anonymous request, so validation and creation must be distinguished.
Touching attributes or calling getId() after invalidate() throws IllegalStateException; caches holding session objects must be dropped on invalidation.
URL-based session tracking (;jsessionid) leaks identifiers into logs and referrers; disable it and require cookies.
maxInactiveInterval is an idle timeout only; an absolute lifetime still has to be enforced by the application.

variants.name: Spring Session over Redis or JDBC (externalized store)
variants.implementation_notes: Spring Session replaces the container-local store with a shared one so any instance validates and invalidates the same session: @EnableRedisHttpSession (Redis 2.8+; the current line requires Java 17 and Servlet 3.1+) or a JDBC store behind the same HttpSession API. Repository lookups and deletes replace the container internals, and findByIndexNameAndIndexValue on the principal-name index supports logout-everywhere. Choose it when several instances must share sessions without sticky routing; the application's own duties (changeSessionId on login, invalidate on logout, attribute serialization) do not change.
pitfalls: @EnableRedisHttpSession relies on Redis keyspace notifications to expire sessions; with notifications disabled, dead sessions linger.
Attributes must be serializable by the chosen serializer; a non-serializable attribute fails at request time, not at build time.
A shared store adds a synchronous round trip to every request and turns a store outage into a total authentication outage; monitor it and cache deliberately.
